sentence_text: Method M outperformed the ZeroGen and SuperGen baselines on both datasets when using the same generator LLM, with the largest gains on SGD (e.g., 72.2% vs 61.3% for Zephyr; 72.4% vs 68.7% for Llama3) and smaller gains on Clinc150 (e.g., 76.0% vs 69.9% for Zephyr; 76.9% vs 73.8% for Llama3).
Method M with open 7-8B generators also surpassed ZeroGen with ChatGPT on both datasets (SGD: 72.2%/72.4% vs 60.2%; Clinc150: 76.0%/76.9% vs 71.3%).

Fine-tuning the rewriter significantly improved accuracy over the non-fine-tuned (NFT) rewriter at the 1x setting across all four dataset/generator combinations (SGD/Zephyr: 72.2% vs 65.0%; SGD/Llama3: 72.4% vs 67.5%; Clinc150/Zephyr: 76.0% vs 73.3%; Clinc150/Llama3: 76.9% vs 73.8%), with significance at alpha=0.05 (one-tailed paired t-test).

The fine-tuning benefit persisted at the 2x setting, with the fine-tuned rewriter outperforming NFT in all four combinations (e.g., SGD/Zephyr: 72.4% vs 62.9%; Clinc150/Llama3: 78.1% vs 76.3%), and these differences were also marked as significant in the source.

Method M achieved the highest Recall@5 among all reranker training objectives on four of the six dataset/backbone combinations (HotpotQA/RankT5, Musique/RankT5, 2WikiHop/RankT5, and 2WikiHop/BGE-Base), with gains of up to 5.7 points over the best LLM-supervised baseline (HotpotQA/RankT5: 84.4 vs 78.7), but it was below the best baseline on HotpotQA/BGE-Base (81.1 vs 81.8) and Musique/BGE-Base (57.6 vs 58.2).

In the generator setting, Method M exceeded the best baseline exact match on four of six configurations (HotpotQA/RankT5, Musique/RankT5, 2WikiHop/RankT5, and Musique/BGE-Base) and was below the best baseline on the remaining two (HotpotQA/BGE-Base and 2WikiHop/BGE-Base).

Because only single runs were performed and no statistical tests were reported, these results do not establish that Method M reliably outperforms the baselines, and the observed differences may not be significant.

Furthermore, the Musique results are limited by the use of random candidate padding to reach 20 documents per query, so the findings may not generalize to settings with naturally larger candidate sets.

On the in-domain Amharic passage retrieval test split, Model M-110M achieves statistically significant improvements (p < 0.05, paired t-test) over the strongest multilingual baseline on MRR@10, NDCG@10, and Recall@10/50/100, with MRR@10 of 0.775 versus 0.672 for multilingual-e5-large-instruct.

The smaller Model M variants (40M and 42M) also outperform all multilingual baselines on the same in-domain metrics, with Model M-42M reaching MRR@10 of 0.735 versus 0.672 for the best baseline, although no significance tests are reported for these comparisons.

This in-domain advantage does not carry over to the separate 2AIRTC collection, where on zero-shot transfer all Model M variants underperform multilingual-e5-large-instruct on MRR@100 and NDCG@100 (e.g., Model M-110M MRR@100 of 0.861 versus 0.905 for the baseline), though no significance markers are given and the collection's sparse/incomplete relevance judgments make recall-based assessments unreliable.

Method M consistently outperformed both ZeroGen and SuperGen baselines on both datasets when using the same generator LLM, with accuracy gains of up to 13.3 percentage points on SGD (72.2 vs 58.9 for Zephyr) and up to 10.2 percentage points on Clinc150 (76.0 vs 65.8 for Zephyr).
Method M with open 7-8B generators also surpassed ZeroGen with ChatGPT on both datasets (e.g., 72.2 vs 60.2 on SGD for Zephyr and 76.9 vs 71.3 on Clinc150 for Llama3).

Fine-tuning the rewriter was crucial: the fine-tuned version significantly outperformed the non-fine-tuned version in all four 1x comparisons (paired t-test, p < 0.05, one-tailed), with gains ranging from 2.7 to 7.2 percentage points.
The significant advantage of fine-tuning persisted when the number of training utterances was doubled (2x), with gains of 1.8 to 9.5 percentage points across all dataset/generator combinations.

On Dataset D, Method M (beam variant) achieved the highest structural adherence to the requested discourse-label sequence, with an automatic Match Score of 0.72 and Levenshtein distance of 0.32, and a human Match Score of 0.55 and Levenshtein distance of 0.17, outperforming all prompting-based baselines (e.g., DeepSeek-V3: auto MS 0.26, human MS 0.24) and the fine-tuned LLaMa-3-8B (auto MS 0.14, human MS 0.18).

This structural gain did not come at a clear cost in content accuracy: Method M (beam variant) achieved a ROUGE-L of 42.98%, FactCC of 0.64, and AlignScore of 0.3890, which is comparable to or better than most prompting baselines (e.g., DeepSeek-V3: ROUGE-L 47.15%, FactCC 0.47, AlignScore 0.3886; GPT-4o: ROUGE-L 29.51%, FactCC 0.63, AlignScore 0.3884).

The edit variant of Method M showed lower content accuracy (ROUGE-L 15.28%, FactCC 0.59) and mixed structural results (auto MS 0.51, human MS 0.24), indicating that the beam variant is the more effective configuration.
No statistical tests were reported, so the observed differences cannot be interpreted as statistically significant, and the results are limited to the single-run, single-dataset setting evaluated.

On Dataset D, Method M (beam variant) achieved the numerically highest structural adherence to the requested discourse-label sequence, with an automatic Match Score of 0.72 and Levenshtein distance of 0.32, and a human Match Score of 0.55 and Levenshtein distance of 0.17, outperforming all prompting-based baselines and the fine-tuned LLaMa-3-8B on these metrics.

This structural gain came with a trade-off in content accuracy: Method M (beam variant) achieved a ROUGE-L of 42.98%, lower than DeepSeek-V3 (47.15%) and LLaMa-3-8B (47.18%), but higher FactCC (0.64 vs. 0.47 and 0.50) and AlignScore (0.3890 vs. 0.3886 and 0.3496).

The edit variant of Method M showed lower content accuracy (ROUGE-L 15.28%, FactCC 0.59, AlignScore not reported) and mixed structural results (auto MS 0.51, human MS 0.24), indicating that the beam variant is the more effective configuration.

No statistical tests were reported, so the observed differences cannot be interpreted as statistically significant, and the results are limited to the single-run, single-dataset setting evaluated, with human structural labels from only 100 summaries per model and two annotators.

Method M-dynamic with FILTER and NN improved COMET over supervised fine-tuning on four of five low-resource pairs (BN, AZ, MN, MR) and on both high-resource pairs (DE, ZH), with gains of up to 1.34 COMET points on BN and 0.65 on DE, while BLEU gains were mixed across low-resource pairs and positive on DE (+1.05) and ZH (+0.08).

Averaged over four languages, Method M-dynamic with FILTER and NN outperformed both REINFORCE and PPO on all four metrics (e.g., BLEU 14.47 vs. 13.88 and 13.94; COMET 70.76 vs. 69.16 and 69.10), and also exceeded supervised fine-tuning on COMET (70.76 vs. 70.02) and XCOMET (60.86 vs. 60.05) but not on BLEU (14.47 vs. 14.11).

Removing the FILTER/NN data techniques from Method M-dynamic reduced averaged BLEU (14.36 vs. 14.47), COMET-KIWI (67.94 vs. 69.97), and XCOMET (59.77 vs. 60.86), indicating that these techniques contribute to the method's gains.

No statistical significance tests were reported, so the observed differences cannot be characterized as statistically reliable, and the results are limited to the specific language pairs, training sizes, and metrics evaluated.

Method M yielded p-values below 0.001 on all four benchmarks (TriviaQA: 1.2e-4, ARC-C: 2.8e-4, MMLU: 7.0e-4, GSM8K: 6.6e-6), whereas PaCoST and LLM DI produced p-values above 0.05 on most benchmarks, indicating that Method M detected contamination more reliably in this setting.

Method M also produced high p-values (0.15–0.73) on held-out subsets of the contaminated model and on an uncontaminated model (0.21–0.55), suggesting it did not flag data the model never saw in these checks.
However, these results are limited to a single model (Pythia-1B) and a single training run, and no statistical tests were reported to support claims of significance or reliability.

Method M-dynamic with FILTER and NN improved COMET over supervised fine-tuning on four of five low-resource pairs (BN, AZ, MN, MR), with gains of up to 5.05 points on MN, but decreased on KA (74.27 vs. 73.92).
On high-resource pairs, Method M-dynamic improved COMET on both DE (79.66 vs. 79.01) and ZH (77.88 vs. 77.71), and improved BLEU on DE (25.29 vs. 24.24) but only marginally on ZH (20.10 vs. 20.02).

Averaged over four languages, Method M-dynamic with FILTER and NN outperformed both REINFORCE and PPO on all four metrics (e.g., BLEU 14.47 vs. 13.88 and 13.94; COMET 70.76 vs. 69.16 and 69.10), and also exceeded supervised fine-tuning on COMET (70.76 vs. 70.02) and XCOMET (60.86 vs. 60.05) but not on BLEU (14.47 vs. 14.11).

Removing the FILTER/NN data techniques from Method M-dynamic was associated with lower averaged BLEU (14.36 vs. 14.47), COMET-KIWI (67.94 vs. 69.97), and XCOMET (59.77 vs. 60.86), suggesting these techniques contribute to the method's gains.

No statistical significance tests were reported, so the observed differences cannot be characterized as statistically reliable, and the results are limited to the specific language pairs, training sizes, and metrics evaluated.

Method M improved COMET scores over supervised fine-tuning on the low-resource pairs AZ, MN, MR, and KA, and BLEU on AZ, MN, and MR, but not on KA (where BLEU was equal or lower), with differences that were small and inconsistent across languages; no significance tests were reported.

On the high-resource pairs, Method M-dynamic improved both BLEU and COMET over supervised fine-tuning for EN-DE (25.29 vs 24.24 BLEU; 79.66 vs 79.01 COMET) and EN-ZH (20.10 vs 20.02 BLEU; 77.88 vs 77.71 COMET), whereas Method M-static did not consistently improve over supervised fine-tuning.

Averaged over four languages, Method M-dynamic with FILTER and NN achieved the highest scores on all four metrics (BLEU 14.47, COMET-KIWI 69.97, COMET 70.76, XCOMET 60.86), outperforming both RL baselines and supervised fine-tuning on COMET-KIWI, COMET, and XCOMET, though not on BLEU where supervised fine-tuning was close (14.11).

The FILTER and NN data techniques contributed to Method M-dynamic's performance, as scores were higher with them than without on all metrics (BLEU 14.47 vs 14.36, COMET-KIWI 69.97 vs 67.94, COMET 70.76 vs 70.23, XCOMET 60.86 vs 59.77).

Method M achieved the highest Recall@5 among the compared reranker training objectives on HotpotQA and 2WikiHop with the RankT5 backbone (84.4 vs. 78.7 and 82.7 vs. 79.2, respectively) and on 2WikiHop with the BGE-Base backbone (81.4 vs. 80.5), but not on Musique with either backbone (57.9 vs. 55.0 for RankT5; 57.6 vs. 58.2 for BGE-Base) nor on HotpotQA with BGE-Base (81.1 vs. 81.8).

In the generator setting, Method M achieved the highest exact match on HotpotQA with RankT5 (61.1 vs. 60.8), on Musique with both backbones (40.0 vs. 39.6 for RankT5; 39.9 vs. 39.7 for BGE-Base), and on 2WikiHop with RankT5 (71.8 vs. 71.6), but not on HotpotQA with BGE-Base (60.9, tied with PDist) nor on 2WikiHop with BGE-Base (70.9 vs. 71.2).

Thus, Method M did not consistently outperform the best LLM-supervised baseline across all datasets and backbones in either reranking quality or answer generation, with its advantage being dataset- and backbone-dependent (e.g., lower Recall@5 on Musique/BGE and HotpotQA/BGE, and lower EM on 2WikiHop/BGE).
These results are based on single runs without variance estimates or significance tests, so the observed differences may not be reliable.

Fine-tuning on self-generated concise reasoning (Method M) reduced output length to 64.25% of the zero-shot baseline on GSM8K and 76.30% on MATH500, while maintaining accuracy within 3 percentage points of the baseline on both datasets (97.00% and 102.56% relative accuracy, respectively).

Compared with other length-reduction approaches, Method M achieved the largest length reduction on both datasets (e.g., 64.25% vs. 67.60% for FT on GPT-4o CoT and 87.17% for naive best-of-N on GSM8K), with comparable or better relative accuracy than these baselines.

The length reduction from Method M did not fully transfer across datasets: models fine-tuned on GSM8K and tested on MATH reduced length to 88.34% of baseline, and models fine-tuned on MATH and tested on GSM8K reduced length to 90.36%, compared with in-domain reductions of 64.25% and 76.30%, respectively.
No statistical tests were reported, so the observed differences in accuracy and length cannot be interpreted as statistically significant or reliable.

In in-domain Amharic passage retrieval, Model M-110M achieved the highest scores on all reported metrics (MRR@10 = 0.775, NDCG@10 = 0.808, Recall@10 = 0.913, Recall@50 = 0.964, Recall@100 = 0.979), with statistically significant improvements over the strongest multilingual baseline (p < 0.05, paired t-test).
The smaller Model M variants (40M and 42M) also outperformed all multilingual baselines on every in-domain metric, indicating a consistent advantage for the Amharic-specific encoders.

However, this advantage did not carry over to the separate 2AIRTC collection: in zero-shot transfer, all Model M variants scored lower than the best multilingual baseline (multilingual-e5-large-instruct) on MRR@100, NDCG@100, and Recall@100, with Model M-110M reaching only 0.861 MRR@100 versus 0.905 for the baseline.

These results suggest that while Amharic-specific training yields strong in-domain retrieval performance, the benefit does not generalize to a different Amharic test collection, possibly due to the sparse and incomplete relevance judgments in 2AIRTC.

Method M achieved larger mean certified radii than the fixed-rate CERT-ED baseline in all three datasets (Yelp: 0.99 vs 0.75; SpamAssassin: 2.86 vs 2.35; LUN: 5.65 vs 4.94), whereas Method M+ showed a mixed pattern, with a substantially larger radius only on LUN (10.69 vs 4.94) and near-parity on Yelp (0.77 vs 0.75) and SpamAssassin (2.77 vs 2.35).

Compared with the fixed-rate RanMASK baseline, Method M achieved larger mean certified radii on all three datasets (Yelp: 0.99 vs 0.61; SpamAssassin: 2.86 vs 2.33; LUN: 5.65 vs 4.83), while Method M+ was larger only on LUN (10.69 vs 4.83) and smaller on Yelp (0.77 vs 0.61) and SpamAssassin (2.77 vs 2.33).

In terms of certified-region cardinality, Method M improved over CERT-ED on SpamAssassin (14.77 vs 14.49) and LUN (38.90 vs 37.68) but not on Yelp (6.89 vs 7.16), whereas Method M+ improved only on LUN (66.90 vs 37.68) and was lower on the other two datasets; against RanMASK, Method M improved on all three datasets (6.89 vs 0.00, 14.77 vs 14.02, 38.90 vs 34.51), while Method M+ improved only on LUN (66.90 vs 34.51) and was lower on Yelp (6.78 vs 0.00) and SpamAssassin (14.01 vs 14.02).

All smoothed methods incurred a substantial clean-accuracy cost relative to NoSmooth (e.g., Yelp: 56.22–57.15% vs 69.25%), and Method M and M+ did not consistently outperform CERT-ED or RanMASK in clean accuracy (e.g., Yelp: 56.98% and 56.22% vs 58.57% and 57.15%).
No statistical tests were reported, so the observed differences in means cannot be interpreted as significant or reliable.

Method M produced lower p-values than PaCoST and LLM DI on all four benchmarks (TriviaQA: 1.2e-4 vs. 1.6e-3, 0.43, 0.02; ARC-C: 2.8e-4 vs. 0.33, 0.31, 0.53; MMLU: 7.0e-4 vs. 0.19, 0.46, 0.03; GSM8K: 6.6e-6 vs. 0.21, 0.30, 0.71), indicating stronger evidence of membership detection in this intentional-contamination setting.

The full Method M also yielded lower p-values than its ablations on all four benchmarks (e.g., TriviaQA: 1.2e-4 vs. 0.14 without paired tests and 0.02 without watermarking), suggesting both the paired-test and watermarking components contribute to detection.

Method M did not flag data the model never saw: all p-values on the uncontaminated model and on held-out subsets of the contaminated model exceeded 0.05 (ranging from 0.07 to 0.73), indicating no false positives in these checks.

These findings are limited to the specific Pythia-1B model, the four benchmarks, and the single contamination setup tested, and no statistical tests or repeated runs are reported, so the reliability of the observed differences cannot be formally established.

Method M achieved the highest average win rate against the seed model at round 5 for both Llama3-8B (73.22% vs. 70.64% for Max-Reward) and Gemma2-2B (66.36% vs. 61.82% for Max-Reward), and it also outperformed all other filtering and scheduling baselines at that round.
However, no statistical tests were reported, so the observed differences in win rates cannot be claimed as significant or reliable.

After the final round, Method M's accuracy on Global MMLU and ARC-C remained close to the seed model for both models (e.g., Llama: 48.90% vs. 48.67% MMLU, 72.28% vs. 72.23% ARC; Gemma: 39.18% vs. 38.88% MMLU, 63.38% vs. 62.85% ARC), indicating no substantial degradation in general knowledge and reasoning.
These results are limited to the two models, ten languages, and five training rounds evaluated, and the absence of significance tests precludes generalizing beyond this specific setup.

Method M improved COMET scores over supervised fine-tuning on most low-resource pairs (AZ, MN, MR, KA) and BLEU on AZ, MN, and MR, but not on BN or KA, with differences that were small and inconsistent across languages.

On the high-resource pairs, Method M-dynamic improved both BLEU and COMET over supervised fine-tuning for EN-DE (25.29 vs 24.24 BLEU; 79.66 vs 79.01 COMET) and EN-ZH (20.10 vs 20.02 BLEU; 77.88 vs 77.71 COMET), whereas Method M-static did not consistently improve over supervised fine-tuning.

The FILTER and NN data techniques contributed to Method M-dynamic's performance, as scores were higher with them than without on all metrics (BLEU 14.47 vs 14.36, COMET-KIWI 69.97 vs 67.94, COMET 70.76 vs 70.23, XCOMET 60.86 vs 59.77).

Fine-tuning on self-generated concise reasoning (Method M) reduced output length more than any other approach on both datasets, to 64.25% of the zero-shot baseline on GSM8K and 76.30% on MATH, but this came with no accuracy gain: relative accuracy was 97.00% on GSM8K and 102.56% on MATH.

The length reduction transferred across datasets but was weaker out-of-domain: training on GSM8K reduced MATH length to 88.34% (vs 64.25% in-domain) and training on MATH reduced GSM8K length to 90.36% (vs 76.30% in-domain), while out-of-domain accuracy remained near baseline (99.21% and 98.53%).

Budget-matched Method M (8+8 paths) produced slightly less length reduction than the full-budget version (16+16) on both datasets (GSM8K: 67.15% vs 64.25%; MATH: 80.43% vs 76.30%) with similar relative accuracy (GSM8K: 97.44% vs 97.00%; MATH: 101.58% vs 102.56%).
No significance tests were reported, and standard deviations were large (e.g., GSM8K relative length SD 16.66 for Method M), so these differences should be interpreted cautiously.

Method M with open 7-8B generators also achieved higher mean accuracy than ZeroGen with ChatGPT on both datasets (e.g., 72.2 vs 60.2 on SGD for Zephyr and 76.9 vs 71.3 on Clinc150 for Llama3).

For this medical-advice prompt, persona instructions can shift outputs, but the effect is not uniform across roles or models: for example, the 'Comedian' persona produced a significant shift in GPT-4 (omega=0.32, p<0.001) and Llama-3.1-8B (omega=0.36, p<0.001), while the 'Doctor' persona produced a significant shift only in Gemma-2-9B (omega=0.41, p<0.01) and Mistral-7B (omega=0.31, p<0.05).

Sensitivity to persona instructions did not consistently differ between larger and smaller models: among the large models, GPT-4 showed significant shifts for two non-medical personas (Comedian, NeurIPS Reviewer) and GPT-3.5 for three (Robot From The Future, NeurIPS Reviewer, Child), while smaller models showed significant shifts for both medical and non-medical personas without a clear pattern.

The audit's sensitivity depended on the embedding model, but the pattern is not uniform: with the default Ada embedding, non-medical personas showed larger effects (e.g., Child omega=0.33, p<0.01), while medical personas under Jasper, Stella, and Kalm embeddings yielded small but significant effects (0.02–0.09), and the generating LLM for these embedding comparisons is unnamed in the source.

In in-domain Amharic passage retrieval, Model M-110M achieved the highest scores on all reported metrics (MRR@10 = 0.775, NDCG@10 = 0.808, Recall@10 = 0.913, Recall@50 = 0.964, Recall@100 = 0.979), with statistically significant improvements over the strongest multilingual baseline (p < 0.05, paired t-test).
The smaller Model M variants (40M and 42M) also outperformed all multilingual baselines on every in-domain metric, indicating a consistent advantage for the Amharic-specific encoders.

In zero-shot transfer to the 2AIRTC collection, no significance testing was reported, and the relative performance of Model M variants versus multilingual baselines varied by metric and baseline: for example, Model M-110M achieved MRR@100 of 0.861 versus 0.905 for multilingual-e5-large-instruct, but on Recall@100 it tied snowflake-arctic-embed-l-v2.0 at 0.830 and exceeded gte-multilingual-base (0.790).

These results suggest that while Amharic-specific training yields strong in-domain retrieval performance, the benefit does not consistently carry over to a different Amharic test collection, though the cause remains untested.

In both evaluated tokenizer-transplant settings, Method M achieved higher scores than the simple (ZeroEmbed, MeanEmbed) and published zero-shot (FOCUS, CLPTransfer, WECHSEL, ZETT) initialization methods on MMLU, ARC-C, GSM8K, and WikiText (e.g., MMLU 0.6222 vs. 0.2299–0.5936 in the Llama 3 → Mistral NeMo setting; 0.3640 vs. 0.2295–0.2695 in the Qwen 2.5 → Llama 3 setting), though no statistical tests were reported for these comparisons.

However, Method M did not fully preserve the original model's performance, showing substantial drops on GSM8K (0.5588 to 0.1289–0.1463 in the 12B setting; 0.0675 to 0.0144 in the 1B setting) and WikiText (0.5296 to 0.7417–0.7798; 0.6605 to 0.7159), with smaller drops on other metrics.
In the high-overlap setting (Qwen 2.5 → Llama 3 1B), Method M performed nearly identically to ZeroEmbed and MeanEmbed, with differences within 0.01 for MMLU, ARC-C, GSM8K, and WikiText.

Increasing the number of anchors from k=8 to k=64 in the low-overlap setting yielded small improvements on most metrics (e.g., MMLU 0.6129 to 0.6222; WikiText 0.7798 to 0.7417), though no statistical tests were reported for any comparison.

Persona instructions can shift language-model outputs for a medical question, but the effect is not uniform across roles or models: for example, the 'Comedian' persona produced a significant shift in GPT-4 (omega=0.32, p<0.001) and Llama-3.1-8B (omega=0.36, p<0.001), while the 'Doctor' persona produced a significant shift only in Gemma-2-9B (omega=0.41, p<0.01) and Mistral-7B (omega=0.31, p<0.05).

The sensitivity to persona instructions did not consistently differ between larger and smaller models: among the large models, GPT-4 showed significant shifts for two non-medical personas (Comedian, NeurIPS Reviewer) and GPT-3.5 for three (Robot From The Future, NeurIPS Reviewer, Child), while smaller models showed significant shifts for both medical and non-medical personas without a clear pattern.

The audit's sensitivity depended strongly on the embedding model: with the default Ada embedding, effect sizes for medical personas ranged from 0.17 to 0.21 and were mostly non-significant, whereas with Jasper, Stella, and Kalm embeddings the same personas yielded much smaller effect sizes (0.02–0.09) that were all statistically significant, indicating that the choice of embedding can change both the magnitude and the significance of detected shifts.

At the 90% deletion rate, Method M achieved a larger mean certified radius than CERT-ED and RanMASK on all three datasets (e.g., Yelp: 0.99 vs. 0.75 and 0.61; SpamAssassin: 2.86 vs. 2.35 and 2.33; LUN: 5.65 vs. 4.94 and 4.83), though its clean accuracy was slightly lower than CERT-ED on Yelp (56.98% vs. 58.57%) and LUN (97.88% vs. 98.20%).
Method M+ produced the largest mean certified radius on LUN (10.69) but not on Yelp (0.77) or SpamAssassin (2.77), where it was lower than Method M and, on Yelp, also lower than CERT-ED (0.75).

Method M+ also achieved the largest certified-region cardinality on LUN (log10 CC = 66.90) and the smallest Wasserstein distance on all three datasets (0.24 each), indicating better adaptation to input length, but on Yelp and SpamAssassin its cardinality was similar to or lower than CERT-ED (6.78 vs. 7.16 and 14.01 vs. 14.49).
All smoothed methods reduced clean accuracy relative to NoSmooth on every dataset, with Method M+ showing the largest drops on Yelp (from 69.25% to 56.22%) and LUN (from 99.16% to 95.09%).

Fine-tuning on self-generated concise reasoning (Method M) reduced output length to 64.25% of the zero-shot baseline on GSM8K and 76.30% on MATH500, with relative accuracies of 97.00% and 102.56%, respectively.

In this comparison, Method M showed the lowest relative length among the evaluated methods on both datasets (e.g., 64.25% vs. 67.60% for FT on GPT-4o CoT and 87.17% for naive best-of-N on GSM8K), but its GSM8K relative accuracy (97.00%) was numerically lower than several baselines, including the 'Be Concise' prompt (99.85%) and Method M-FS (99.94%).

The length reduction did not fully transfer across datasets: relative to the zero-shot baseline on each test set, models fine-tuned on GSM8K and tested on MATH reduced length to 88.34%, and models fine-tuned on MATH and tested on GSM8K reduced length to 90.36%, compared with in-domain reductions of 64.25% and 76.30%, respectively.
No statistical tests were reported, so the observed differences in accuracy and length cannot be interpreted as statistically significant or reliable.

Adding Method M to each of the three evaluated KD losses (GKD, KLD, SRKL) improved average ROUGE-L across the five instruction-following sets, with gains of 2.33, 1.60, and 1.51 points respectively, and the improvement was consistent on every individual dataset for each loss.

The ablation with KLD shows that the full Method M (with both the rising temperature and the decaying supervised-loss ratio) yields the highest scores on all five datasets, while removing the ratio schedule (keeping only the temperature schedule) reduces performance on four of five datasets, and removing both schedules (keeping only the easy-to-hard curriculum) performs comparably to plain KLD on average.

These results are limited to the GPT-2 family, the three KD losses and five evaluation sets tested, and no statistical significance tests were reported, so the consistency and size of the improvements cannot be formally established.

In the generator setting, Method M matched or exceeded the best baseline exact match on five of six configurations, with the largest improvement on HotpotQA/RankT5 (61.1 vs 60.8), while on 2WikiHop/BGE-Base it was slightly below LOOP (70.9 vs 71.2).

Because only single runs were performed and no statistical tests were reported, these results do not establish that Method M reliably outperforms the baselines, and the observed differences may not be significant.

Method M achieved the highest reported win rate at round 5 for both Llama3-8B (73.22% vs. 70.64% for Max-Reward) and Gemma2-2B (66.36% vs. 61.82% for Max-Reward), and also led at rounds 3 and 4 for Gemma2-2B (65.54% and 69.22%) but not for Llama3-8B at round 3 (66.58% vs. 67.23% for Max-Reward).
No statistical tests were reported, so the observed differences in win rates cannot be claimed as significant or reliable.

After the final round, Method M's accuracy on Global MMLU and ARC-C remained within 0.3–0.5 percentage points of the seed model for both models (e.g., Llama: 48.90% vs. 48.67% MMLU, 72.28% vs. 72.23% ARC; Gemma: 39.18% vs. 38.88% MMLU, 63.38% vs. 62.85% ARC), though no tests confirm equivalence.
These results are limited to the two models, ten languages, and five training rounds evaluated, and the absence of significance tests precludes generalizing beyond this specific setup.

Method M produced lower p-values than PaCoST and LLM DI on all four benchmarks (TriviaQA: 1.2e-4 vs. 1.6e-3, 0.43, 0.02; ARC-C: 2.8e-4 vs. 0.33, 0.31, 0.53; MMLU: 7.0e-4 vs. 0.19, 0.46, 0.03; GSM8K: 6.6e-6 vs. 0.21, 0.30, 0.71) in this intentional-contamination setting; no statistical test is reported for this comparison, so the reliability of the differences is not formally established.

The full Method M also yielded lower p-values than its ablations on all four benchmarks (e.g., TriviaQA: 1.2e-4 vs. 0.14 without paired tests and 0.02 without watermarking), suggesting both the paired-test and watermarking components contribute to detection.

Method M did not flag data the model never saw: all p-values on the uncontaminated model and on held-out subsets of the contaminated model exceeded 0.05 (ranging from 0.07 to 0.73), indicating no false positives in these checks.

These findings are limited to the specific Pythia-1B model, the four benchmarks, and the single contamination setup tested, and no statistical tests or repeated runs are reported, so the reliability of the observed differences cannot be formally established.

Method M produced p-values below 0.001 on all four benchmarks (TriviaQA: 1.2e-4, ARC-C: 2.8e-4, MMLU: 7.0e-4, GSM8K: 6.6e-6), whereas PaCoST and LLM DI (same) yielded p-values above 0.05 on most benchmarks, with the exception of LLM DI (different) on TriviaQA (0.02) and MMLU (0.03).

In false-positive checks, Method M produced p-values above 0.05 on all uncontaminated benchmarks (0.21–0.55) and on most held-out subsets (0.15–0.73), except for Abstracts (0.07), which fell below the conventional 0.05 threshold.

These results are limited to a single model (Pythia-1B), a single training run, and 1,000-example subsamples per benchmark, and no statistical tests were reported to support claims of significance or reliability.

Adding Method M to each of the three evaluated KD losses (GKD, KLD, SRKL) improved average ROUGE-L across the five instruction-following sets, with gains of 2.33, 1.60, and 1.51 points respectively, and the improvement was observed on every individual dataset for each loss.

The ablation with KLD shows that the full Method M (with both the rising temperature and the decaying supervised-loss ratio) yields the highest scores on all five datasets, while removing the ratio schedule (keeping only the temperature schedule) reduces performance on all five datasets, and removing both schedules (keeping only the easy-to-hard curriculum) performs comparably to plain KLD on average.

These results are limited to the GPT-2 1.5B-to-0.1B setting, the three KD losses and five evaluation sets tested, and no statistical significance tests were reported, so the consistency and size of the improvements cannot be formally established.

Method M achieved the highest average win rate on the aya evaluation suite at the final round for both models, reaching 73.22% for Llama3-8B and 66.36% for Gemma2-2B, surpassing the strongest other filter Max-Reward (70.64% and 61.82%, respectively).

However, Method M's advantage over Max-Reward was not consistent across earlier rounds: at R3 and R4, Method M was lower for Llama3-8B (66.58% vs 67.23% at R3; 69.99% vs 70.39% at R4) but higher for Gemma2-2B (65.54% vs 63.73% at R3; 69.22% vs 67.72% at R4).

After the final round, Method M did not degrade general knowledge and reasoning accuracy relative to the seed model, with Global MMLU and ARC-C accuracies of 48.90% and 72.28% for Llama3-8B (seed: 48.67% and 72.23%) and 39.18% and 63.38% for Gemma2-2B (seed: 38.88% and 62.85%).

On Global MMLU, Method M's accuracy was not uniformly the best among filters: for Llama3-8B it was lower than Mult-Full, Rand, Min-Len, and Max-Len (48.90% vs 49.47%, 49.23%, 50.62%, 49.78%) but higher than Max-Reward (48.28%); for Gemma2-2B it was lower than Mult-Full, Max-Len, and Max-Reward (39.18% vs 40.48%, 41.80%, 42.48%) but higher than Rand and Min-Len (39.73%, 37.00%).

Method M (beam variant) achieved higher structural adherence than all prompting baselines and the fine-tuned model, with the highest automatic Match Score (0.72 vs. 0.11–0.26) and lowest automatic Levenshtein distance (0.32 vs. 0.64–0.80), and also the highest human Match Score (0.55 vs. 0.15–0.24) and lowest human Levenshtein distance (0.17 vs. 0.49–0.65).

The beam variant did not show a consistent content-accuracy cost relative to prompting baselines: its ROUGE-L (42.98%) was lower than DeepSeek-V3 (47.15%) and LLaMa-3-8B (47.18%) but higher than Claude (34.30%), GPT-4o (29.51%), and Qwen-2.5 (40.82%); its FactCC (0.64) was higher than all prompting baselines (0.47–0.70) except Claude (0.70), and its AlignScore (0.3890) was comparable to or higher than all prompting baselines (0.3496–0.3888).

The edit variant of Method M showed lower structural adherence than the beam variant on automatic metrics (auto MS 0.51 vs. 0.72; auto Lev 0.48 vs. 0.32) and much lower human Match Score (0.24 vs. 0.55), with higher human Levenshtein distance (0.65 vs. 0.17), and it had substantially lower ROUGE-L (15.28% vs. 42.98%) while FactCC was similar (0.59 vs. 0.64).

Fine-tuned LLaMa-3-8B did not improve structural adherence over vanilla LLaMa-3-8B: it had lower automatic Match Score (0.14 vs. 0.21) and lower human Match Score (0.18 vs. 0.24), with equal automatic Levenshtein distance (0.77) and higher human Levenshtein distance (0.55 vs. 0.49), and it also had much lower ROUGE-L (22.01% vs. 47.18%).

Method M consistently achieved larger mean certified radii than the fixed-rate CERT-ED baseline across all three datasets (Yelp: 0.99 vs 0.75; SpamAssassin: 2.86 vs 2.35; LUN: 5.65 vs 4.94), while Method M+ showed a mixed pattern, with a larger radius only on LUN (10.69 vs 4.94) and smaller radii on Yelp (0.77 vs 0.75) and SpamAssassin (2.77 vs 2.35).

In terms of certified-region cardinality, Method M improved over CERT-ED on SpamAssassin (14.77 vs 14.49) and LUN (38.90 vs 37.68) but not on Yelp (6.89 vs 7.16), whereas Method M+ improved only on LUN (66.90 vs 37.68) and was lower on the other two datasets.

The clean-accuracy cost of certification was substantial for all smoothed methods relative to NoSmooth (e.g., Yelp: 56.98–57.15% vs 69.25%), and Method M and M+ did not consistently outperform CERT-ED in clean accuracy (e.g., Yelp: 56.98% and 56.22% vs 58.57%).
No statistical tests were reported, so the observed differences in means cannot be interpreted as significant or reliable.

In the Llama 3 to Mistral NeMo 12B transplant (54% vocabulary overlap), Method M with k=64 outperformed FOCUS and the simple baselines on most metrics, but not on WikiText (0.7417 vs. 0.9881 for ZeroEmbed and 0.8993 for MeanEmbed) or GSM8K (0.1463 vs. 0.0334 and 0.0523).

In the Qwen 2.5 to Llama 3 1B transplant (86% overlap), Method M (k=64) matched or slightly exceeded the published zero-shot methods and the simple baselines on most metrics, with performance nearly identical to ZeroEmbed and MeanEmbed (e.g., MMLU 0.3640 vs. 0.3640 and 0.3641; WikiText 0.7159 vs. 0.7169 and 0.7180).

Method M did not fully preserve the original model's performance: in the 12B transplant, it fell short on all metrics, with the largest relative drop in GSM8K (0.1463 vs. 0.5588), and in the 1B transplant it showed smaller gaps on MMLU and ARC-C but a substantial drop in GSM8K (0.0144 vs. 0.0675) and a modest increase in WikiText (0.7159 vs. 0.6605 bits/byte).
No statistical tests were reported, so the significance of these differences cannot be assessed.

In both evaluated tokenizer-transplant settings, Method M's benchmark scores were higher than those of the simple (ZeroEmbed, MeanEmbed) and published zero-shot (FOCUS, CLPTransfer, WECHSEL, ZETT) initialization methods on MMLU (e.g., 0.6222 vs. 0.2299–0.5936 in the Llama 3 → Mistral NeMo setting; 0.3640 vs. 0.2295–0.2695 in the Qwen 2.5 → Llama 3 setting), though no statistical tests were reported for these comparisons.

However, Method M did not fully preserve the original model's performance, showing substantial drops on GSM8K (0.5588 to 0.1289–0.1463 in the 12B setting; 0.0675 to 0.0144 in the 1B setting) and WikiText (0.5296 to 0.7417–0.7798; 0.6605 to 0.7159), with smaller drops on other metrics.
In the high-overlap setting (Qwen 2.5 → Llama 3 1B), Method M performed nearly identically to ZeroEmbed and MeanEmbed, with differences within 0.01 for MMLU, ARC-C, GSM8K, and WikiText.

Increasing the number of anchors from k=8 to k=64 in the low-overlap setting yielded small improvements on most metrics (e.g., MMLU 0.6129 to 0.6222; WikiText 0.7798 to 0.7417), though no statistical tests were reported for any comparison.

Method M reported higher accuracy than the ZeroGen and SuperGen baselines on both datasets when using the same generator LLM, with the largest reported gains on SGD (e.g., 72.2% vs 61.3% for Zephyr; 72.4% vs 68.7% for Llama3) and smaller gains on Clinc150 (e.g., 76.0% vs 69.9% for Zephyr; 76.9% vs 73.8% for Llama3); no significance test was reported for these comparisons.
Method M with open 7-8B generators also surpassed ZeroGen with ChatGPT on both datasets (SGD: 72.2%/72.4% vs 60.2%; Clinc150: 76.0%/76.9% vs 71.3%).

Fine-tuning the rewriter significantly improved accuracy over the non-fine-tuned (NFT) rewriter at the 1x setting across all four dataset/generator combinations (SGD/Zephyr: 72.2% vs 65.0%; SGD/Llama3: 72.4% vs 67.5%; Clinc150/Zephyr: 76.0% vs 73.3%; Clinc150/Llama3: 76.9% vs 73.8%), with significance at alpha=0.05 (one-tailed paired t-test).

The fine-tuning benefit persisted at the 2x setting, with the fine-tuned rewriter outperforming NFT in all four combinations (e.g., SGD/Zephyr: 72.4% vs 62.9%; Clinc150/Llama3: 78.1% vs 76.3%), and these differences were also marked as significant in the source.

Adding Method M to each of the three evaluated KD losses (GKD, KLD, SRKL) improved average ROUGE-L across the five instruction-following sets, with gains of 2.33, 1.60, and 1.51 points, respectively, and also improved scores on most individual datasets.

The component ablation with KLD shows that the supervised-ratio schedule is the main driver of the improvement: removing it (keeping only the temperature schedule) yields scores close to or below plain KLD (e.g., DollyEval 22.04 vs 23.49, SelfInst 8.70 vs 10.33), whereas removing the temperature schedule (keeping the ratio schedule) retains most of the gain (e.g., DollyEval 24.33, UnNI 23.87).

The best distilled student with Method M (SRKL + Method M) outperformed the teacher on two of five datasets (VicunaEval 16.66 vs 16.47, S-NI 28.49 vs 27.66) but not on the other three or on average (22.94 vs 23.44).

No statistical tests or standard deviations are reported, so the significance and consistency of these gains cannot be established, and the findings are limited to the GPT-2 family and the five evaluated instruction-following sets.

In the Llama 3 to Mistral NeMo 12B transplant (54% vocabulary overlap), Method M with k=64 outperformed all baselines on every reported metric, achieving MMLU 0.6222, ARC-C 0.5273, XNLI 0.3780, GSM8K 0.1463, AGIEval 0.3158, Lambada 0.6895, and WikiText 0.7417 bits/byte, whereas FOCUS collapsed to near-zero accuracy on several tasks (e.g., Lambada 0.0000, WikiText 5.8441).

In the Qwen 2.5 to Llama 3 1B transplant (86% overlap), Method M (k=64) matched or exceeded all published zero-shot methods on every metric, with MMLU 0.3640, ARC-C 0.3626, GSM8K 0.0144, Belebele 0.2704, and WikiText 0.7159, while CLPTransfer, FOCUS, WECHSEL, and ZETT all performed worse, with CLPTransfer producing a WikiText of 6791.6044 bits/byte.

However, Method M did not fully preserve the original model's performance: in the 12B transplant, the original model achieved MMLU 0.6452, ARC-C 0.5811, XNLI 0.4367, GSM8K 0.5588, AGIEval 0.3752, Lambada 0.7819, and WikiText 0.5296, while Method M (k=64) fell short on all metrics, with the largest relative drop in GSM8K (0.1463 vs. 0.5588).

In the 1B transplant, Method M (k=64) closely matched the original model on MMLU (0.3640 vs. 0.3673) and ARC-C (0.3626 vs. 0.3626) but showed a substantial drop in GSM8K (0.0144 vs. 0.0675) and a modest increase in WikiText (0.7159 vs. 0.6605 bits/byte).
